exercises.prompt: Implement rowSums(matrix), where matrix is an array of rows and each row is an array of numbers, so it returns an array with the sum of each row — rowSums([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) is [3, 7]. Rows may have different lengths, and an empty row sums to 0. An empty matrix returns an empty array.
hints: You want one number per row, so map over the rows and collapse each one to its sum.
Inside the map, sum a row with reduce: row.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0).
return matrix.map(row => row.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0)) — the 0 seed makes an empty row sum to 0.

exercises.prompt: Implement flattenOnce(matrix) so it merges the rows of matrix into a single array, one level deep — flattenOnce([[1, 2], [3], [4, 5]]) is [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Only one level is removed: an element that is itself an array stays nested. Empty rows contribute nothing, and an empty matrix returns an empty array.
hints: Flattening joins the inner arrays end to end into one array.
arr.flat() removes exactly one level of nesting — which is all this asks for.
return matrix.flat() — because it peels only one level, an element that is itself an array stays an array.

exercises.prompt: Implement columnAt(matrix, c) so it returns column c of the matrix as an array — the element at index c taken from each row. columnAt([[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]], 0) is [1, 3, 5]. Assume every row has an element at index c. An empty matrix returns an empty array.
hints: A column is one element taken from every row — so produce one value per row again.
map each row to its element at index c: row => row[c].

exercises.prompt: Implement gridMax(matrix) so it returns the largest number anywhere in the matrix, across all rows. gridMax([[1, 9], [3, 4]]) is 9. Assume the matrix holds at least one number, though rows may vary in length. The values may all be negative.
hints: The largest cell could be in any row, so it helps to consider all the numbers together.
flat() merges the grid into one array; Math.max(...arr) then finds the biggest — the spread ... passes the array's numbers as separate arguments.
return Math.max(...matrix.flat()) — this stays correct even when every value is negative.

exercises.prompt: Implement transpose(matrix) so it swaps the rows and columns of a rectangular matrix: the first row of the result is the first element of each original row, and so on. transpose([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]) is [[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]]. Assume the matrix has at least one row, every row has the same length, and that length is at least one.
hints: The result has one row per original column, and each new row gathers that column's value from every original row.
Build one output row per column index c, each row being matrix.map(row => row[c]); the number of columns is matrix[0].length.
return matrix[0].map((_, c) => matrix.map(row => row[c])) — mapping over the first row gives you a c for each column.
